content: The 2016 update to the WHO guidelines for the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) introduced several key recommendations and changes based on the latest evidence. These updates were designed to optimize treatment regimens for patients with rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB), multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), as well as for those with Mycobacterium bovis disease. Below are the key points presented in a clear and professional manner: 1. Optimal Treatment Regimens for Drug-Resistant TB: The guidelines provide recommendations for the composition of treatment regimens for adults and children with RR-TB, MDR-TB, and XDR-TB. These regimens aim to maximize efficacy while minimizing toxicity. For patients with isoniazid-resistant TB, the evidence was insufficient to address specific treatment questions, and no new recommendations were made. 2. Shorter MDR-TB Regimens: A shorter treatment regimen lasting 9–12 months may be used for patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB who have not been previously treated with second-line drugs and in whom resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents is unlikely or excluded. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low certainty in the evidence. 3. Longer MDR-TB Regimens: For patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB, a longer regimen should include at least five effective TB medicines during the intensive phase. This includes pyrazinamide and four core second-line TB medicines: one from Group A (fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, or gatifloxacin), one from Group B (injectable agents such as amikacin, capreomycin, or kanamycin), and at least two from Group C (ethionamide/prothionamide, cycloserine/terizidone, linezolid, or clofazimine). If the minimum number of effective medicines cannot be achieved, agents from Group D2 (bedaquiline, delamanid) and Group D3 (p-aminosalicylic acid, imipenem-cilastatin, meropenem, amoxicillin-clavulanate) may be added to reach a total of five medicines. 4. Strengthening Regimens: High-dose isoniazid and/or ethambutol may be added to further strengthen the regimen for patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty in the evidence. 5. Treatment of Children: Specific recommendations are provided for the treatment of children with RR-TB or MDR-TB. In cases of non-severe disease, Group B medicines (injectable agents) may be excluded. 6. Surgical Interventions: Elective partial lung resection (lobectomy or wedge resection) may be considered as an adjunct to a recommended MDR-TB regimen for patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low certainty in the evidence. 7. Reclassification of Medicines: The grouping of medicines used in MDR/RR-TB treatment has been revised to reflect updated evidence on their efficacy and safety. Clofazimine and linezolid are now recommended as core second-line medicines, while p-aminosalicylic acid is classified as an add-on agent. 8. Use of Bedaquiline and Delamanid: Bedaquiline is recommended only for adults, while delamanid may also be used in patients aged 6–17 years. These two medicines now occupy a unique subgroup within the add-on agents for MDR/RR-TB treatment. 9. Policy Continuity: The 2016 update does not revise certain aspects of the 2011 recommendations, such as the use of rapid diagnostics for RR-TB, monitoring of treatment response, and the duration of longer MDR-TB regimens. These earlier recommendations remain valid until new evidence necessitates further updates. 10. Evidence Basis: The recommendations are informed by systematic reviews, meta-analyses of individual patient data, and aggregated data from observational studies conducted in various regions, including Asia and Africa. For children, the recommendations are based on pediatric-specific data from studies published up to September 2014. 11. Implementation and Future Updates: The guidelines emphasize the importance of accompanying remarks and context for proper implementation. Future evidence reviews will determine whether additional revisions to the WHO policy are required. These updates aim to support healthcare professionals worldwide in addressing the challenges posed by drug-resistant TB, particularly in the context of the End TB Strategy. The recommendations reflect the latest evidence on the medical and surgical management of drug-resistant TB in both adults and children.
